newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Donnelley bolsters troubled unit.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Donnelley bolsters troubled unit.

text.p: Donnelley Enterprise Solutions Inc said it will see some fallout in the first quarter from problems that plagued its LANSystems division in 1996, but it expects the situation to be resolved by the second quarter.

"We will see a little carryover as we get the (new) engineers up to speed in the first quarter, but in the second quarter we believe we'll be back on track," chief financial officer Luke Botica told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Donnelley's outlook for 1996 earnings substantially below analysts' estimates put its stock in a tailspin Thursday.
Shares in the Chicago-based provider of information management services were off 11-1/4 to 12-1/2. Donnelley was spun off last November from R.R. Donnelley & Sons Co.
"That's clearly a disappointment," Botica said of the stock's slide. But he said Donnelley Enterprise has taken steps to fix its problems, which he described as mainly related to labor.

LANSystems, accounting for about 45 percent of the company's business, in the fourth quarter was hit with higher operating costs due to use of extensive subcontracted help. The subcontractors were needed to accommodate demand that outstripped in-house staffing capacity.

"We kicked up our hiring, and our recruiting efforts are paying off," Botica said. At year-end 1996, the division had 121 engineers, up from 96 in June 1996. That number should rise to about 138 by the end of the second quarter, he added.
Training of newly hired engineers in the fourth quarter caused efficiency and productivity to suffer, Botica said.

To beef up LANSystems' performance, the company in January named Robert Lento division president. In addition, Botica said, Donnelley Enterprise is centralizing its controller function and accounting processes.

Donnelley Enterprise said Thursday it expects 1996 net income to be between $600,000 and $900,000. "That's $0.12 to $0.18 a share for the year," said Botica, adding that analysts were projecting about $0.39 a share.

LANSystems provides information technology services, such as systems integration, consulting and software development. Donnelley Enterprise's other main businesses are office services outsourcing and information systems, such as computer desktop support and system management.

Commenting on the sharp falloff in the stock, Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp said, "The company reported a substantial shortfall compared to analysts' estimates. But the decline in the stock seems to be somewhat overdone."
Donnelley Enterprise said Montgomery Securities lowered its rating on the stock to hold from buy. The analyst was not available for comment.
